cues.text: From Reader in Rome to Bishop of Vercelli
Born on Sardinia around 283, Eusebius was taken to Rome by his mother after his father's martyrdom, where he served for a time as a lector in the Roman church.
In 340, he was unanimously elected bishop of Vercelli in northern Italy by its clergy and people, and received episcopal consecration from Pope Julius I that same year.
The First Monk-Bishop of the West
According to St. Ambrose 's own testimony, Eusebius was 'the first bishop of the West who united monastic with clerical life.'
He organized his cathedral clergy into a common life modeled on the practices of the Eastern monks.
This pioneering fusion of monasticism and diocesan ministry led later Canons Regular of St. Augustine to honor him as a founding inspiration.
Legate to a Hostile Emperor
In 355, Pope Liberius sent Eusebius, alongside Bishop Lucifer of Cagliari, as a legate to plead the cause of St. Athanasius before Emperor Constantius II at a council in Milan.
Rather than sign the emperor's demanded condemnation of the great Nicene defender, Eusebius refused outright, a defiance that led to his own exile.
Years of Exile
Eusebius's banishment carried him first to Scythopolis in Syria, where a hostile Arian bishop watched him.
Eusebius himself described that bishop as his jailer.
He was then sent further still to Cappadocia and finally to the Thebaid in Upper Egypt.
There, he endured years of hardship and even physical mistreatment for refusing to abandon Nicene orthodoxy.
Return and Final Years

Freed upon the accession of Emperor Julian in 361, Eusebius traveled through the East working to reconcile factions divided by the Arian controversy, including a difficult mission to Antioch, before finally returning to his own see at Vercelli in 363.
There he joined St. Hilary of Poitiers in continuing the broader campaign against Arianism in the West until his death around 371.
Legacy
Eusebius is honored by the Church as a confessor of the faith for his years of exile and hardship endured rather than betray Nicene doctrine.
His pioneering combination of monastic discipline with active diocesan ministry left a lasting institutional legacy in the later tradition of Canons Regular.
That tradition continues to claim him, alongside St. Augustine, as a founding father.
